def: The palpable dip at the top of the sternum between the clavicles. A thrill here, or a murmur radiating to it, can indicate aortic valve disease.
An antiprotozoal drug used for Giardia and Cryptosporidium infection, especially in immunocompetent patients.
A thick-walled structure filled with endospores formed by Coccidioides in tissue. Identified on microscopy in coccidioidomycosis (valley fever).
A semisynthetic bile acid that activates the farnesoid X receptor, used for primary biliary cholangitis. Can cause pruritus.
Yeast-like buds formed by Candida, which can elongate into pseudohyphae.
A broad-spectrum azole antifungal used for invasive aspergillosis and mucormycosis.
A polymer in the gram-positive bacterial cell wall that anchors to the membrane and induces cytokine release by the host (TLR2).
An amino sugar that alternates with N-acetylmuramic acid to form bacterial peptidoglycan, the target of beta-lactams and lysozyme.
An amino sugar that alternates with N-acetylglucosamine in bacterial peptidoglycan and carries the peptide side chains that become cross-linked.
A test in which antibodies against a bacterial capsule make the capsule swell and appear refractile under the microscope. Used for encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus.
A short hair-like bacterial surface appendage used for attachment to host cells and surfaces, e.g., E. coli to the urinary tract. Plural fimbriae.
A DNA segment that can move between locations in a genome or between plasmids and chromosomes. In bacteria, can carry antibiotic resistance genes.
A bedside test of light touch using a thin nylon filament pressed on the foot, used to detect diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
A microscopy method in which organisms appear bright on a dark background, used to see thin spirochetes such as Treponema pallidum in syphilis.
Syphilis screening blood tests (VDRL, RPR) that detect antibodies to cardiolipin released from damaged cells. Sensitive but can be falsely positive in lupus and other conditions.
Relating to a gumma, a soft granulomatous lesion with a firm necrotic center, characteristic of tertiary syphilis.
The effect of a drug or influence on heart rate. Positive chronotropy speeds the heart; negative slows it.
A CFTR corrector that helps misfolded F508del CFTR protein reach the cell surface. Used with ivacaftor in cystic fibrosis.
A CFTR potentiator that keeps the chloride channel open longer on the cell surface, used for cystic fibrosis with certain mutations.
Relating to large blood vessels. Macrovascular complications of diabetes include coronary, cerebral and peripheral artery disease.
An interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis infection measuring T cell response to TB antigens in blood. Not affected by BCG vaccination.
A mycobacterial enzyme that builds arabinogalactan in the cell wall. Blocked by ethambutol.
Located above the medial epicondyle of the elbow. Epitrochlear lymph nodes enlarge in infections of the hand and forearm, and in secondary syphilis.
A drug that increases urinary excretion of uric acid, such as probenecid, used in gout.
Relating to the neck and face. Cervicofacial actinomycosis is a chronic jaw infection with draining sinuses and yellow sulfur granules.
Affecting a single joint. Acute monoarticular arthritis requires joint aspiration to exclude septic arthritis and crystal disease.
Low serum complement levels (C3, C4), caused by consumption in immune complex diseases such as lupus nephritis and cryoglobulinemia.
Relating to tophi, deposits of monosodium urate crystals in joints, ears and soft tissue in chronic gout.
A grating or crackling sensation or sound from joints, bone fragments or air under the skin.
The state of awareness and orientation of a patient. Clouded sensorium suggests delirium.
Addition of an adenylyl (AMP) group to a molecule. Adenylating enzymes can inactivate aminoglycosides.
Transferring an ADP-ribose group from NAD onto a protein. Toxins such as pertussis, cholera and diphtheria toxin act this way.
A fluorescent yellow-green pigment made by Pseudomonas aeruginosa that scavenges iron.
Mulberry-like cytoplasmic clusters of bacteria in white blood cells, seen in ehrlichiosis (monocytes) and anaplasmosis (granulocytes).
The family of negative-sense RNA viruses that includes respiratory syncytial virus and human metapneumovirus.
Tapering of the subglottic airway on a neck x-ray, resembling a church steeple, seen in croup.
The virus family of hepatitis D, a defective RNA virus that needs hepatitis B surface antigen to replicate.
Without jaundice. Many hepatitis A infections in children are anicteric.
An intermediate formed from PABA and pteridine by dihydropteroate synthase, on the bacterial folate pathway blocked by sulfonamides.
To slip between stacked base pairs of DNA, distorting it and blocking replication and transcription. Done by dactinomycin and doxorubicin.
Overwinding or underwinding of the DNA double helix on itself. Topoisomerases relieve it during replication; gyrase introduces negative supercoils.
A second-generation BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for chronic myeloid leukemia.
A MEK inhibitor given with a BRAF inhibitor for BRAF V600E-mutant melanoma.
The tendency of cancer cells to make ATP by glycolysis and lactate fermentation even when oxygen is available.
A fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme that converts lanosterol to ergosterol. Inhibited by azole antifungals.
By injection into the subarachnoid space around the spinal cord, delivering a drug directly to cerebrospinal fluid.
Stopping fungal growth without killing the organism, as with griseofulvin.
The rapidly dividing form of Toxoplasma gondii that spreads in tissues during acute infection.
Relating to the choroid and retina. Chorioretinitis is a feature of congenital toxoplasmosis and CMV infection.
The sexual stage of malaria and some other parasites, taken up by the mosquito to continue the life cycle.
The flagellated, motile form of Leishmania found in the sandfly vector. It is the infective form that enters humans.
Occurring every day. In malaria, fevers every 24 hours; tertian fevers occur every 48 hours and quartan every 72.
Roundworms, nonsegmented helminths with a complete digestive tract. Examples include Ascaris, Enterobius (pinworm) and hookworm.
Transient, localized, nonpitting swellings of the limbs caused by migrating adult Loa loa worms.
Flatworms known as flukes, with complex life cycles involving a snail host. Includes Schistosoma and liver flukes.
Having a lid (operculum). The eggs of Clonorchis sinensis are small and operculated.
Relating to typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi or paratyphi, as opposed to non-typhoidal Salmonella that cause gastroenteritis.
Worsening of confusion, agitation and disorientation in the late afternoon or evening, common in dementia and delirium.
A radiograph of the esophagus after swallowing contrast (barium). Shows a bird's beak in achalasia.
Surgical or endoscopic removal of dead pancreatic tissue, used in infected necrotizing pancreatitis.
An x-ray of the bile ducts with contrast injected, used to find stones or strictures. Can be done through ERCP.
Affecting four or fewer joints. Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the most common type in children.
Lacking a capsule that can be typed; nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae is unencapsulated and not covered by the Hib vaccine.
A multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown cause, with noncaseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, elevated ACE and hypercalcemia.
